name: Eggplant
summary: How most Filipino farmers raise talong: seedlings grown in a seedbed for about a month, then set out in furrowed rows and picked twice a week for months. It is written for small farms in the lowlands and uplands that grow talong for the market or for the home.
season: Talong grows all year in the Philippines wherever there is water for the dry months. In the lowlands the main crop is usually set out after the rice harvest and grown through the dry season, and a wet season crop is planted on raised rows with wider gaps between hills so water drains away.
material: Seed, about 100 to 200 grams for a hectare (one gram holds roughly 250 seeds). Farmers soak the seed in clean water overnight, dry it in the air, and sow it in a seedbed or in trays, then move the seedlings to the field when they are about 30 to 35 days old with 3 to 4 true leaves. Many still make their own seedling cups by rolling strips of banana leaf and pinning them with a broom stick.
spacing: Rows 75 to 100 cm apart and about 50 cm between hills, one seedling a hill. In the wet season many farmers widen the gap between hills to about 75 cm. Two rows are often set on one bed so the leaves shade the fruits.
water: Furrow irrigation: water is let into the furrows and allowed to soak in, never left standing. In the dry season farmers water about a week after planting, near 21 and 30 days, then every 10 days or so. In the wet season only when the soil dries. In the seedbed, farmers water early in the day and only enough to keep the soil from drying.
fertilizer: Dried chicken manure or compost before planting, about 5 tons for a hectare, then a tablespoon of 14 14 14 in each hole at planting. Urea and muriate of potash, about 15 grams each a plant, between 10 and 15 days after planting, urea again near 30 days, and small doses of urea, potash or 14 14 14 every few weeks while the plants are bearing. Some pour the fertilizer as a answer, a sardine can full a hill.
care: Off barring at 14 to 21 days and hilling up at 21 to 35 days, with hand weeding between plants. Low side shoots are pruned off below the first fork, and each plant gets a bamboo stake. Rice straw is spread as mulch where it is at hand. Farmers cut off wilted shoot tips and bored fruits every week, pull and burn plants that wilt and die, and some plant marigold or lemongrass at the edges of the field to keep insects away.
harvest: The first fruits are ready about 46 to 50 days after transplanting for hybrids and closer to 70 days for open pollinated kinds. Pick young, shiny, firm fruits before the seeds harden, early in the morning, with a knife or shears, twice a week for 3 to 5 months. Sort out damaged fruits and pack the rest in a lined kaing, crate or pin holed plastic bag, out of the sun and rain.

ways.label: Transplanted from a seedbed (lipat tanim)

steps.title: Clean the seedbed soil
steps.how: Make beds about 1 meter wide and 15 cm high in a sunny spot near water. Wet the bed, cover it with 3 to 5 cm of rice straw or rice hull and burn it slowly to kill weed seeds and soil diseases. Rake off the ash and wait a few days before sowing.

steps.title: Soak and sow the seed
steps.how: Soak the seed overnight and let it dry in the air. Draw shallow lines 5 cm apart with a stick, drop the seed thinly along them and cover with fine soil, or sow one seed a hole about 1 cm deep in a tray filled with equal parts compost, burnt rice hull and garden soil. Water gently.
steps.tip: A slanted roof of cogon, coconut leaves or old sacks over the bed keeps off hard sun and heavy rain.

parts.title: Soak overnight, then air dry
parts.how: Soak the seed in clean water overnight so it sprouts sooner. Spread it on a cloth or paper in the shade until it no longer sticks together in the fingers.

parts.title: Roast the soil for the trays
parts.how: For trays or small pots, roast the garden soil over a fire, stirring it, to kill the fungi, insects and weed seed in it. Let it cool, then a day later mix it with equal parts of compost and burnt rice hull.

parts.title: Fill the trays
parts.how: Fill the cells of a tray with 100 or 104 holes with the mix and press it down lightly. Ready mixed seedling media from farm stores work too.

parts.title: Sow one seed a cell, or in lines
parts.how: In trays, drop one seed in each cell about 1 cm deep, cover with fine soil and sprinkle with water. On a seedbed, water the bed first, mark lines about 5 cm apart with a stick, drop the seed evenly along them and cover with fine soil.

parts.title: Water in the morning, not too much
parts.how: Give water early in the day and only enough that the soil stays damp. Too much water brings damping off and thin, weak seedlings.

parts.title: Put up a slanted shade
parts.how: Build a simple roof of cogon, talahib, coconut leaves or old plastic sacks over the beds or trays. Make the east posts taller, about 120 cm, and the west posts about half that, around 60 cm, so the morning sun reaches the seedlings but the hot afternoon sun and hard rain do not.

steps.title: Thin and prick out
steps.how: A few days after the seedlings come up, or when they show 2 to 3 leaves, pull out the crowded ones. Move the extras into trays, banana leaf cups or another bed, water them and keep them in the shade until they perk up.

parts.title: Thin them early
parts.how: Three to five days after the seedlings come up, or when they show their first two or three leaves, pull out the crowded ones and keep the strongest. The extras go into cups or trays.
parts.time: 3 to 5 days after they come up

parts.title: Make banana leaf cups
parts.how: Cut banana leaves into strips about two inches wide, roll each strip into a small ring and pin the ends with a broom stick (tingting) so it does not open. Stand the cups side by side inside a square wooden frame.

parts.title: Fill the cups and move the seedlings
parts.how: Fill the cups with a mix of 2 parts compost, 1 part soil and 1 part burnt rice hull. Poke a hole in each, set one seedling in it, holding it by a leaf, and firm the soil around it.

parts.title: Water and shade until they perk up
parts.how: Water the moved seedlings right away and keep them under the shade until they stand up again. At planting time each seedling leaves its cup with a whole ball of soil, so the roots are hardly disturbed.

steps.title: Plow and harrow the field
steps.how: Plow 15 to 20 cm deep two or three times, a week apart, and harrow after each pass to break the clods. This gives old stubble and weeds time to rot.

steps.title: Give the seedlings a starter drink
steps.how: Dissolve about 2 tablespoons of 16 20 0 or 14 14 14 in 4 liters of water and pour it over the seedlings. Rinse the leaves with plain water right after so they do not burn. Water only in the morning and only enough to keep the soil damp.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: Take the shade off a little longer each day, starting with the morning sun, and water less often. By the end of the week the seedlings should stand the whole day of sun without wilting badly.

parts.title: Start with the morning sun
parts.how: On the first day of the last week before planting, take the shade off and let the seedlings stand in the sun until about ten in the morning, then cover them again.

parts.title: Add more sun each day
parts.how: Leave the cover off a little longer every day, until the seedlings can take the sun the whole day.

parts.title: Give less water
parts.how: At the same time, water a little less and less often. Seedlings that are not soaked every day grow tougher stems and roots.

parts.title: Do not let them wilt hard
parts.how: A little drooping at noon is normal. If the seedlings wilt badly, shade them and water them, then go on more slowly.

steps.title: Make the rows and work in manure
steps.how: Open furrows or raised rows 75 to 100 cm apart. Spread dried chicken manure or compost along them, about 5 tons for a hectare, and mix it into the soil.

steps.title: Transplant in the late afternoon
steps.how: Lift the seedlings with the soil still on their roots and set one in each hill, 50 cm apart in the dry season and up to 75 cm in the wet season. Mix about a tablespoon of 14 14 14 into the bottom of each hole first, then plant and water right away.
steps.tip: Many farmers set two rows on one bed so the leaves shade the hanging fruits from sun scald.

steps.title: Replant missing hills
steps.how: Walk the rows 3 to 5 days after planting and replace dead or badly wilted seedlings with spares from the seedbed.

steps.title: First furrow irrigation
steps.how: In the dry season let water run down the furrows about a week after planting, again near 21 and 30 days, then every 10 days or so. Do not let water stand around the stems.

steps.title: First side dressing
steps.how: Between 10 and 15 days after planting, give each plant about 15 grams of urea and 15 grams of muriate of potash. Drop it in a shallow groove a hand span from the stem and cover it with soil.

steps.title: Off bar and pull weeds
steps.how: Plow or hoe the soil away from the rows between 14 and 21 days after planting to kill young weeds. Hand pull the weeds left between the plants.

steps.title: Prune the low shoots
steps.how: Remove the side shoots that grow below the first fork of the stem, keeping the one branch nearest the fork. Cut off old yellow leaves too, and do it in the morning so the cuts dry fast.

steps.title: Hill up and stake
steps.how: Plow or hoe the soil back against the rows between 21 and 35 days after planting. Push a bamboo stake beside each plant and tie it loosely so the plant does not fall when it is heavy with fruit.

steps.title: Check for borer and wilt every week
steps.how: Look for wilted shoot tips and fruits with small holes. Cut them off, gather them in a sack and destroy them away from the field. Pull and burn any plant that wilts suddenly and dies, since that is a soil disease.

steps.title: Second side dressing
steps.how: About a month after planting, give each plant another 15 grams of urea in a groove beside the row and cover it. Water the furrow afterwards if the soil is dry.

steps.title: Start picking
steps.how: Pick the fruits while they are young, glossy and firm, early in the morning, using a knife or shears so the branch is not torn. Pick every ready fruit twice a week to keep the plant bearing.

steps.title: Sort and pack
steps.how: Set aside damaged and crooked fruits. Pack the good ones in a kaing or crate lined with old paper and dry banana leaves, or in plastic bags with two pin holes for each kilo, and keep them out of the sun.

steps.title: Keep seed from the best plants
steps.how: Farmers who keep their own seed of an open pollinated variety leave a few fruits on the best plants to ripen fully, then take out the seed, dry it slowly and store it dry and cool.

parts.title: Mark the seed fruits
parts.how: Pick out strong, healthy plants that bear well and true to the variety. Tie a string on a few well shaped fruits and leave them on the plant past eating stage.

parts.title: Wait for yellow to brown
parts.how: Pick the seed fruits only when the skin has turned yellow to brown and the fruit has gone soft. Seed from green fruit is not ripe and sprouts poorly.

parts.title: Slice and scrape out the seed
parts.how: Press and roll the fruit to loosen the seed, slice it open lengthwise and scrape the seed out. Wash it in water and throw away the seeds that float with the pulp.

parts.title: Air dry, then sun dry
parts.how: Spread the seed on a screen or put it in a net bag and dry it in the shade, where air moves, for at least three days. Then finish it in the sun for up to five days.
parts.time: at least 3 days in the shade, then up to 5 days in the sun

parts.title: Store it dry and cool
parts.how: Keep the dry seed in sealed plastic bags or glass jars, labeled with the variety and date, in the coolest, driest corner of the house.

steps.title: Feed again while it bears
steps.how: While picking goes on, give a small dose of urea or muriate of potash every few weeks, or about a tablespoon of 14 14 14 a plant later in the season. Some farmers dissolve the fertilizer in water and pour a sardine can full at each hill.

ways.note: Hybrids give the first fruits about 46 to 50 days after transplanting. Open pollinated kinds take closer to 70 days. Picking then goes on twice a week for about 3 to 5 months.

mistakes: Watering the seedbed too much, which brings damping off and weak, leggy seedlings.
Leaving water standing in the furrows, which rots the roots and spreads wilt.
Planting talong again where talong, tomato or pepper just grew, so wilt builds up in the soil.
Spraying for fruit and shoot borer on a fixed calendar instead of cutting out the damaged shoots and fruits each week.
Skipping or delaying the side dressing, which gives weak plants and small fruits.
Leaving old fruits on the plant, which slows down new flowers and fruits.
better: Have the soil tested and feed by the result. Lime acid soil so it sits near pH 5.5 to 6.8.
Buy good seed of a variety that resists bacterial wilt, or use seedlings grafted onto a wilt resistant rootstock.
Raise seedlings in trays with a clean mix so every seedling has its own root ball and fewer die after transplanting.
Use silver plastic mulch or thick rice straw mulch to cut weeding and save water.
Fight fruit and shoot borer with weekly removal of damaged parts, sex pheromone traps and spraying only when the count is high.
Rotate with rice, corn or a bean crop, not with tomato, pepper or potato.

watering.traditional: Talong is watered by furrow: water is let into the furrows between the rows, allowed to soak in and never left standing. In the dry season farmers water about a week after transplanting, again near 21 and 30 days, then about every 10 days for as long as they pick. In the wet season only when the soil dries.
watering.method: Furrow irrigation from a canal, a shallow well or a small pump is the usual way. Small growers water each hill with a can or a hose. Plastic mulch with water let into the furrows is common on commercial farms. Water in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Set out the main crop after the rice harvest so it starts on the moisture left in the field, and mulch with rice straw or rice hull to hold it. Without a canal, carry water by can or pail to each hill when the soil dries during flowering, and choose a field near a well or creek.
watering.dryseason: Furrow irrigate about a week after transplanting, near 21 and 30 days, then about every 10 days until picking ends, more often on sandy soil. Water when the leaves droop by mid morning or the soil a few cm down feels dry.
watering.wet: Plant on raised rows with wider gaps between hills, about 75 cm, so water drains and air moves. Water only when the soil dries. Soaked soil brings root rot and bacterial wilt, which makes whole plants droop and die.

schedule.often: Water the bed before sowing, sprinkle the trays after sowing, then water each morning
schedule.amount: Just enough to keep the soil damp, never soggy
schedule.why: Overwatered seedbeds bring damping off and thin, weak seedlings.

schedule.often: Water in the morning only, enough to keep the soil moist. Water and shade the pricked seedlings until they recover
schedule.amount: Light sprinkles. Rinse the leaves with plain water right after the starter drink
schedule.why: Steady, light water grows sturdy seedlings, and fertilizer left on the leaves burns them.

schedule.often: Water less and less often while the shade comes off
schedule.amount: Light waterings. Water at once if they wilt hard
schedule.why: Seedlings used to less water and full sun take the move to the field better.

schedule.often: With plastic mulch, flood the beds two days before transplanting. Without mulch, water the furrows before or at planting
schedule.amount: Soak the beds or rows through
schedule.why: Water cools the soil under the mulch and dissolves the base fertilizer so it does not burn the young roots.

schedule.often: Water each hill right after transplanting. In hot weather give wilting hills a little water by can until the first furrow irrigation
schedule.amount: Soak the soil around each seedling
schedule.why: Newly set seedlings root only in moist soil. Dead or wilted ones are replaced at 3 to 5 days.

schedule.often: In the dry season, furrow irrigate at about 7, 21 and 30 days after transplanting
schedule.amount: Let water run down the furrows until the rows are wet, then let it soak in with none left standing
schedule.why: A big, well rooted plant carries more fruits for the months of picking.

schedule.often: About every 10 days in the dry season, or whenever the soil dries. Water after each feeding
schedule.amount: The plants use about 3.5 to 4 cm of water a week in dry weather, so each watering should soak the rows well
schedule.why: Dry soil drops flowers and gives small, crooked, bitter fruits, while soaked soil rots roots and spreads wilt.

critical: The first week after transplanting, while the seedlings root.
Flowering and fruit growth: steady moisture keeps flowers from dropping and fruits from turning small and crooked.
All season: water must never stand around the stems, because talong is easily hurt by flooding.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and roll in the heat, flowers fall before setting, and fruits stay small, crooked or turn dull and bitter.
signs.wet: Lower leaves yellow and drop, plants wilt suddenly while the soil is wet, and the stems turn soft or brown inside at the base.

better: Lay a mulch of plastic, rice hull or straw over the beds: the soil stays damp longer, fewer weeds come up and you may water only half as often.
A drip line under the mulch gives each plant the steady water talong needs through months of picking with far less water than flooding.
